feedback.problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}+6x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{{x}^{2}+6x}) \\  & ={({x}^{2}+6x)}^{′}{e}^{{x}^{2}+6x} \\  & =(2x+6)\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+6)\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+6x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{{x}^{2}+6x}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by ${e}^{{x}^{2}+6x}$ and solve the resulting equation. 

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+6)\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+6x} & =0 \\ 2x+6 & =0 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has a stationary point at $x=-3.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical point of $f(x)$ is $x=-3.$
